summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly; local legislator Orlando Smith said at the time that "there is nothing we can do."

The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume that United Kingdom discrimination and service-access protections, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under British Virgin Islands law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.

No criminalisation of trans people, and no trans-specific protection machinery, appears in the sources for the territory. The visitor-relevant legal questions are the framework relationship with the United Kingdom and the unsettled recognition of marriages contracted elsewhere.
tangentialFactors:
GlobalGayz, in assessments published in 2012 and 2017, rated the British Virgin Islands among the more welcoming islands in the Caribbean for gay people while describing local homophobia as "silent and invisible" and gay life there as lived in secret. The assessment is not trans-specific and predates the current decade.

The Privy Council's order covered five British Caribbean territories; the British Virgin Islands' position on decriminalisation is shared with neighbouring jurisdictions in the region rather than unique to it.
localsOnly:
The litigation over recognition of a marriage contracted in the United Kingdom is the principal resident-facing legal question. The BVI Christian Council's bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack was refused on 29 July 2022, which cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised.

No British Virgin Islands legislation specific to transgender people, and no local hate-crime or protection machinery for them, appears in the sources.
